body:
Why does nuclear power require special safety measures?

A nuclear reactor uses controlled fission to release energy, but the process also produces radioactive materials. These materials must be kept from causing harmful radiation exposure or contaminating the environment.

Many fission products, formed when heavy nuclei split, are unstable. They undergo radioactive decay and emit radiation until they transform into more stable nuclei.

During normal operation, nuclear fuel is enclosed within protective material, and additional barriers are provided to prevent radioactive substances from escaping into the environment.

What happens when the reactor is shut down?

Stopping the main fission chain reaction does not make all heat production disappear immediately.

Even after the reactor is shut down, radioactive fission products continue to decay. Their decay releases energy in the form of decay heat.

Decay heat is different from the heat produced by the continuing main fission chain reaction:

  • Fission heat: The principal heat produced during normal reactor operation by the splitting of heavy nuclei.
  • Decay heat: Heat released as unstable radioactive nuclei undergo subsequent radioactive decay, including after the chain reaction has been stopped.

Therefore, cooling remains necessary after reactor shutdown. The amount of decay heat decreases with time, but it does not become zero immediately.

Shutdown does not mean immediate absence of heat. The chain reaction can be stopped while radioactive decay continues. Continued heat removal is an essential part of nuclear safety.

Basic safety principles

Three broad safety functions are important in understanding nuclear power generation:

  • Control the nuclear reaction: Maintain the chain reaction at the required rate and stop it when necessary.
  • Remove heat: Prevent excessive heating of the fuel during operation and after shutdown.
  • Confine radioactive materials: Use protective barriers and radiation shielding to reduce the risk of harmful releases and exposure.

Protective barriers and shielding serve a different purpose from control rods. Control rods primarily influence the availability of neutrons for fission. Shielding and containment help protect people and the environment from radiation and radioactive materials.

Benefits and limitations of nuclear electricity

Nuclear power can provide substantial electricity from a relatively small quantity of fuel. It can also generate electricity continuously without depending directly on daily sunlight or wind conditions.

Unlike coal combustion, the fission reaction itself does not release carbon dioxide through the burning of carbon-based fuel. However, emissions can arise from other stages of a nuclear plant's life cycle, including construction and fuel-related activities.

Nuclear power also has important limitations:

  • Uranium is a finite mineral resource, so conventional uranium-based nuclear energy is classified as non-renewable.
  • Used nuclear fuel and some other wastes contain radioactive materials that require controlled handling and storage.
  • Reliable cooling, radiation protection and prevention of accidental releases remain essential.

Used nuclear fuel is not necessarily devoid of useful material, but its handling requires specialised procedures because it remains radioactive and can continue producing decay heat.

Prelims focus

  • Many fission products are radioactive.
  • Decay heat continues after the main fission chain reaction stops.
  • Cooling remains necessary after reactor shutdown.
  • Control rods regulate the reaction, while shielding and containment provide radiation protection.
  • Conventional uranium-based nuclear power is non-renewable.
  • Trap: Stopping fission does not immediately stop radioactive decay.

[Sources: IAEA, 'Glossary of terms', entries 'Decay Heat', 'Decay, Radioactive', 'Control Rod' and 'Coolant', consulted 16 November 2026; IAEA, 'Fundamentals of Nuclear Power', section 'Fission Products and Nuclear Poisoning', consulted 16 November 2026; Atomic Energy Regulatory Board, public information booklet on nuclear power plant safety, section 'Maintenance of core cooling', p. 21; NPCIL, Corporate Profile 2025, section 'Major Attributes of Nuclear Power', printed p. 2; NCERT, Science, Class 10, 2020–21 edition, chapter 14, section 14.3.4, printed pp. 251–252.]

title: Radioactive Products, Reactor Shutdown and Basic Nuclear Safety

body:
Two different ways of releasing nuclear energy

Both nuclear fission and nuclear fusion can release large amounts of energy through changes within atomic nuclei.

However, they involve opposite types of nuclear transformation.

In fission, a heavy nucleus splits into lighter nuclei. In fusion, light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus.

Nuclear fission: splitting a heavy nucleus

A typical nuclear fission reaction used for power production begins when a U-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron. The nucleus splits, releasing energy and additional neutrons.

The released neutrons can sustain further fission reactions. This is the physical basis of the controlled chain reaction in conventional nuclear power reactors.

U-235 is an important fissile isotope. Plutonium-239 is another example of a fissile nuclear material, although the details of its use depend on the reactor type.

Nuclear fusion: combining light nuclei

In nuclear fusion, 2 light atomic nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus. A widely studied example uses the hydrogen isotopes deuterium and tritium.

Their fusion produces a helium nucleus, a neutron and energy.

Fusion requires conditions under which the positively charged nuclei can overcome their electrical repulsion sufficiently to combine. This generally involves extremely high temperatures.

Fusion powers the Sun and other stars. The conditions within stars allow light nuclei to undergo fusion and release enormous amounts of energy.

Comparison of fission and fusion

BasisNuclear fissionNuclear fusion
Basic processHeavy nucleus splits into lighter nucleiLight nuclei combine into a heavier nucleus
Typical materialsU-235; also Pu-239 in suitable systemsHydrogen isotopes such as deuterium and tritium
Characteristic conditionCan be induced by neutron absorptionRequires extremely high temperatures
Familiar exampleConventional nuclear power reactorsSun and other stars
Electricity generationCommercially establishedStill under research and development for commercial power

Why is fusion not used in ordinary nuclear power stations?

A controlled fission chain reaction can release heat continuously within established commercial reactor technology.

Fusion presents different scientific and technological challenges. The extremely hot material involved in fusion must be maintained under suitable conditions long enough for useful energy production, and that energy must then be recovered for practical use.

As of the 16 November 2026 content cutoff, commercial electricity generation from nuclear fusion has not become an established operating technology. Conventional commercial nuclear power stations generate electricity through nuclear fission.

The US Department of Energy's fusion roadmap, released on 9 June 2026, describes further scientific and technological development directed towards future commercial fusion power. Its proposed development timeline is a goal, not evidence that commercial fusion generation is already operating.

Fission: One heavy nucleus splits. Fusion: Light nuclei combine. Both release nuclear energy, but existing commercial nuclear electricity generation is based on fission.

Prelims focus

  • Fission involves the splitting of heavy nuclei.
  • Fusion involves the combination of light nuclei.
  • U-235 is a typical fuel isotope for neutron-induced fission.
  • Deuterium and tritium are hydrogen isotopes studied for fusion.
  • Fusion is the principal energy-producing nuclear process in the Sun.
  • Trap: Ordinary commercial nuclear power stations do not produce electricity through solar-type fusion reactions.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 10, 2020–21 edition, chapter 14, 'Sources of Energy', section 14.3.4 and the accompanying 'Nuclear fusion' discussion, printed pp. 251–252; US Department of Energy, 'Fusion Energy', section explaining fusion and commercialisation challenges, updated 17 June 2026, consulted 16 November 2026; US Department of Energy, 'Energy Department Releases Finalized Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap to Accelerate Commercial Fusion Power', published 9 June 2026, consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: U-235 absorbs a neutron and splits; deuterium and tritium join to form helium. Both processes release neutrons and energy.
pictures.caption: Fission divides a heavy nucleus; fusion combines light nuclei.

title: Nuclear Fission versus Nuclear Fusion

body:
The nuclear fuel resources of India

Uranium and thorium are important minerals associated with nuclear energy. However, their nuclear properties are not identical.

Uranium contains the fissile isotope U-235, which can sustain a chain reaction when suitable neutrons are available.

The principal naturally occurring thorium isotope, thorium-232 (Th-232), is different. It is a fertile material: it can be converted through nuclear reactions into a fissile material, uranium-233 (U-233). Thorium-232 is therefore not a direct substitute for U-235 as a fuel that readily undergoes fission with slow neutrons.

Fissile versus fertile: U-235 is fissile and can sustain neutron-induced fission. Th-232 is fertile and requires conversion into a fissile isotope before it can serve that role.

Important uranium and thorium locations

Uranium resources

Uranium resources occur in several parts of India. Important geographical associations include:

  • Jharkhand: Uranium occurrences in the Singhbhum Copper Belt, including the Jaduguda region.
  • Andhra Pradesh: The Tummalapalle uranium deposit in the Kadapa region.
  • Rajasthan: Uranium occurrences in districts including Udaipur, Alwar and Jhunjhunu.

These are examples of important locations, not an exhaustive list of uranium deposits or operating mines.

Thorium resources

Thorium is associated particularly with monazite-bearing beach sands along parts of India's coast.

Kerala and Tamil Nadu are important locations for these deposits. Monazite-bearing coastal deposits also occur in other parts of peninsular India.

The resource distinction is important: uranium is used in established nuclear power generation, whereas the large-scale use of India's thorium resources involves additional fuel-conversion technology.

Important nuclear power stations and their states

For geographical identification, the location of a nuclear power station should be associated with its state rather than with the location of uranium or thorium deposits.

Nuclear power stationState
Kakrapar Atomic Power StationGujarat
Tarapur Atomic Power StationMaharashtra
Rajasthan Atomic Power Station, RawatbhataRajasthan
Madras Atomic Power Station, KalpakkamTamil Nadu
Narora Atomic Power StationUttar Pradesh
Kaiga Generating StationKarnataka
Kudankulam Nuclear Power StationTamil Nadu

These are important examples of Indian nuclear power stations, not a complete inventory of all reactors or proposed nuclear projects.

Gujarat connection: Kakrapar Atomic Power Station

Kakrapar Atomic Power Station (KAPS) is located in the Surat district of Gujarat. It is operated by the Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL).

Kakrapar is particularly relevant to understanding India's pressurised heavy-water reactor technology. The station uses PHWR units, a reactor type associated with natural uranium fuel and heavy water as moderator and coolant.

According to NPCIL's operating-performance information, the Kakrapar units are:

UnitReactor typeElectrical capacity
KAPS-1PHWR220 MWe
KAPS-2PHWR220 MWe
KAPS-3PHWR700 MWe
KAPS-4PHWR700 MWe

The station's total listed electrical capacity is 1,840 MWe. Here, MWe means megawatts of electrical generating capacity, as distinct from thermal power produced inside a reactor.

Data period and status: NPCIL's operating-performance page, consulted for the 16 November 2026 content cutoff, identifies KAPS-1 to KAPS-4 as operating units. The page displays generation statistics for April–July 2026 within the 2026–27 financial year. The unit capacities stated above are installed-capacity figures, not generation during that period.

Connecting nuclear resources with electricity generation

The basic chain of understanding is that nuclear fuel contains suitable fissile nuclei, controlled fission releases heat, the reactor coolant transfers that heat, and the steam-turbine-generator system produces electricity.

India's PHWR technology illustrates how these principles are applied using natural uranium and heavy water. Kakrapar provides a direct example of this technology within Gujarat.

Thorium is an important potential nuclear energy resource, but its fertile nature means it must not be confused with the U-235 that directly sustains neutron-induced fission in conventional thermal reactors.

Prelims focus

  • Uranium resources are associated with Jharkhand, Andhra Pradesh and Rajasthan.
  • Thorium is associated with monazite-bearing coastal sands, notably in Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
  • Kakrapar Atomic Power Station is in Surat district, Gujarat.
  • Kakrapar has 220 MWe units and 700 MWe units, all of PHWR type.
  • Indian PHWRs generally use natural uranium fuel and heavy water as moderator and coolant.
  • Trap: Thorium-232 is fertile, not directly fissile like U-235.

[Sources: NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, older edition, chapter 'Mineral and Energy Resources', section 'Nuclear Energy Resources', printed pp. 80–82; Department of Atomic Energy, 'UCIL Commissions Uranium Mining and Processing Plant at Tummalapalle, Andhra Pradesh', 20 April 2012; Department of Atomic Energy, 'Export of Monazite from India: Facts', 19 October 2012; NPCIL, Corporate Profile 2025, section 'Long-Term Nuclear Power Programme of the Country', printed p. 3; NPCIL, Kakrapar Atomic Power Station, 'Operating Performance', unit-capacity and commercial-operation table and FY 2026–27 generation table covering April–July 2026, consulted 16 November 2026; IAEA, 'Thorium: An Alternative Fuel for Nuclear Energy', IAEA Bulletin, September 2023, section 'Challenges of thorium for energy production'.]
